"Do in" is a phrasal verb — a main verb ("do") combined with a small particle ("in") that together produce a meaning you cannot guess just from the two words alone. This is what makes phrasal verbs tricky for learners: "do" means one thing on its own, and "in" means another, but together they create something new.

"Do in" is informal and colloquial, meaning it belongs in everyday speech, casual writing, texts, films, and novels — not in formal essays or professional emails.

It has four distinct meanings. All four share the same dark thread: bringing something to a ruinous, painful, or final end — whether that end is a person's life, your physical energy, your body, or someone's reputation.

Meaning 1 — To Kill Someone

This is the most dramatic meaning and the one most associated with crime fiction, thrillers, and gangster films.

"To do someone in" = to kill them, usually deliberately.

It is slang. It is not as clinical or formal as "murder" or "kill." It carries a slightly gritty, storytelling quality — the kind of language a detective novel uses.

Examples:

  • "The hitman was paid to do the witness in."
  • "Nobody knew who had done the old banker in."
  • "She was done in by her own business partner."
  • "They waited for the right moment and then did him in."

What to notice:

  • The past tense "did [someone] in" is very natural.
  • The passive "was done in" is also extremely common — it emphasises the victim, not the killer.
  • You will almost always hear this used about a person, not an animal or object.

Meaning 2 — To Exhaust Someone Completely

This is by far the most common meaning in everyday life. You will hear this constantly in British English, and regularly in other varieties too.

"To do someone in" = to leave them feeling completely and utterly drained — not just tired, but wiped out, with nothing left to give.

The exhaustion is total. This is not mild tiredness. It is the feeling after something physically or mentally brutal.

Examples:

  • "That 12-hour shift at the hospital totally did me in."
  • "Three back-to-back exams have really done her in."
  • "I'm absolutely done in after moving all those boxes." (Here "done in" works as a describing word meaning "completely exhausted.")
  • "The long climb up the mountain did us all in."
  • "Even just one hour of intense revision does him in."

What to notice:

  • "Done in" used on its own (without an object) acts like an adjective: "I'm done in" = "I'm completely wiped out."
  • The exhausting thing is usually a task, event, or experience — not a person.
  • This meaning is especially popular in British English, but it is well understood everywhere.

Meaning 3 — To Ruin or Destroy Someone (Career, Reputation, Chances)

This meaning is about downfall, not physical harm. It describes something that ends a person's career, destroys their reputation, or permanently ruins their prospects.

"To do someone in" = to bring about their ruin or failure.

Examples:

  • "The corruption scandal did the politician in." (= It ended his career.)
  • "His terrible temper eventually did him in at that company." (= It caused his downfall there.)
  • "One careless tweet did her in with the sponsors." (= It ruined that relationship.)
  • "The bad harvest and poor planning together did in the business." (= Together they destroyed it.)

What to notice:

  • The cause of the ruin is often not a person but a situation, a flaw, a mistake, or an event.
  • This meaning is about permanent damage — once someone is "done in" in this sense, they don't easily recover.
  • You can use it about a business, project, or plan — not just a person.

Meaning 4 — To Injure a Part of Your Body

This meaning is especially common in British and Australian English, though speakers of other varieties will understand it too.

"To do [a body part] in" = to hurt or injure it, usually through strain, overuse, or accident.

Examples:

  • "I did my back in lifting those heavy boxes."
  • "She did her knee in during the football match."
  • "He did his shoulder in at the gym last week."
  • "Be careful with that ladder — you'll do your ankle in."

What to notice:

  • The body part always sits between "do" and "in": "did my back in," "did her knee in."
  • The injury is typically from overexertion, awkward movement, or accident — not from someone attacking you (that would be Meaning 1).
  • This meaning feels very natural and conversational in British speech.
Grammar — How to Use "Do In" Correctly

"Do in" is what linguists call a separable phrasal verb. This means the object (the person or thing affected) can go between "do" and "in," or it can go after "in."

Rule 1 — When the object is a pronoun (me, him, her, them, us, it):
The pronoun must go between "do" and "in." You cannot put it after "in."

✅ "It did him in." (correct)
❌ "It did in him." (sounds wrong and unnatural)

✅ "That run did me in." (correct)
❌ "That run did in me." (sounds wrong)

Rule 2 — When the object is a noun or noun phrase:
You have a choice. Both positions work.

✅ "The scandal did the minister in."
✅ "The scandal did in the minister."

Both are grammatically fine. The first (object in the middle) tends to feel slightly more natural in speech.

Rule 3 — Passive voice:
The passive form is very common with "do in," especially for Meanings 1 and 2.

The passive is formed with "be done in":

  • "He was done in by his rivals." (killed)
  • "She was completely done in after the race." (exhausted)
  • "The project was done in by poor management." (ruined)
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Being Used

Since "do in" has four meanings, you need context to identify the right one. Here are your four quick clues:

Someone is dead, or there is talk of killing → Meaning 1 (kill)
"The body was found. Someone had done him in."

Someone is exhausted after effort or hardship → Meaning 2 (exhaust completely)
"I'm done in after that gym session."

Someone's career, reputation, or plans are ruined → Meaning 3 (ruin/destroy)
"One bad decision did her in professionally."

A specific body part is mentioned → Meaning 4 (injure a body part)
"I've done my wrist in."

The meanings are distinct enough that confusion is rare in real speech. Context almost always makes it crystal clear.

"Do in" conjugates exactly like the verb "do":

  • Present: "This kind of work does me in."
  • Past simple: "That long hike did me in."
  • Present perfect: "The scandal has done him in."
  • Past perfect: "The injury had done her in long before the final."
  • Future: "This exam will do me in."
  • Continuous (less common but possible): "The heat is slowly doing us in."

"Do in" is solidly informal. Here is a simple breakdown:

Use it freely in:
Everyday conversation, text messages, casual emails to friends, fiction writing, film and TV dialogue, journalism (especially in informal or headline style).

Avoid it in:
Formal essays, academic writing, professional reports, official documents, business correspondence.

If you need a more formal equivalent, here are substitutes for each meaning:

  • Meaning 1 (kill): murder, kill, assassinate, eliminate
  • Meaning 2 (exhaust): exhaust, fatigue, drain, wear out
  • Meaning 3 (ruin): ruin, destroy, bring down, cause the downfall of
  • Meaning 4 (injure a body part): injure, strain, damage
A Brief Note on Why "In" Is There

This is a natural question. Why "in"? In many phrasal verbs, "in" carries a sense of finality or completion — bringing something all the way through to its end. Think of "hand in," "turn in," "fill in," "cash in" — the "in" often signals that something is being brought to a concluded state. In "do in," the "in" amplifies "do" to mean doing something all the way through, to a complete, often irreversible end. This is why all four meanings share that sense of something being finished off.

Knowing these nearby expressions helps you understand "do in" more fully and shows you how it fits into the broader family of English idioms:

"Done for" — completely ruined, with no hope left.
"After losing all his savings, he was done for."
(Similar to Meaning 3, but even more final and hopeless.)

"Finish off" — to kill or completely use up something; also to complete something.
"The frost finished off the remaining crops."
(Overlaps with Meaning 1.)

"Knock out" — to exhaust completely (informal).
"That run knocked me out."
(Overlaps with Meaning 2.)

"Worn out" — exhausted, depleted.
"I'm completely worn out."
(Synonym of the Meaning 2 result — but "worn out" describes a state, while "do in" describes the action that caused it.)

"Do away with" — to get rid of something or someone; can mean to kill, but is slightly more formal than "do in."
"He threatened to do away with his competitor."

"Bust up" — to injure (body), or to break a relationship (informal, common in British/Australian English).
"I've busted up my hip."
(Overlaps loosely with Meaning 4.)

"Do in" is a separable, informal phrasal verb with four meanings:

1. To kill — deliberate, used in crime and thriller contexts. "They did him in."

2. To exhaust completely — the most everyday use; total physical or mental depletion. "That shift did me in."

3. To ruin or destroy — bringing an end to someone's career, reputation, or plans. "His arrogance did him in."

4. To injure a body part — common in British and Australian English; the body part goes between "do" and "in." "I did my back in."

It is always informal. The object goes between "do" and "in" when the object is a pronoun. Context — especially what comes around the phrase — will always tell you which of the four meanings is at play.
